utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So good morning, Madam Registrar. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. I notice that accused Nikolic is not present in the courtroom. We have been informed that he will be present later on. At the moment he's got some medical appointment. Otherwise the Defence teams are all here, and everyone is present. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey for the time being. For the time being. I had asked you yesterday if you have any response to the Prosecution submission to convert Witness 68 from viva voce to 92 ter witness and for protective measures for that witness. Are there any objections on the part of any of the Defence teams? We hear none. So the motion is granted -- is granted. So, Mr. McCloskey. Good morning to you, Witness. Welcome back. We are going to proceed with your testimony today and hopefully try to finish. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. If we could pull up that 65 ter 1563 photo again, but while that's coming up, let me take you briefly back to the meadow near Sandici. You said there was a military tank there. Do you remember any other big military machines or weapons around the meadow while you were there that day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally there were, yes. And there was a Praga near us to the right. There was a tank in our vicinity. There was a mobile anti-aircraft gun, 20/3 millimetre with three barrels, and it was on the road or near the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What's the difference between a Praga and this mobile anti-aircraft weapon you just described?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Praga had its position; it was dug in somewhat. I wasn't sure whether it was mobile or not. I'm not quite sure whether it could move, whether it had wheels. It was positioned in a -- in a housing or in a base, and the same applied to the tank and to the anti-aircraft gun. All of them were facing with their barrels towards the woods from which we had come.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you know what kind of barrels the Praga had?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It had two barrels. A tank has one barrel, an anti-aircraft gun has three barrels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How is it that you know about these sorts of weapons?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about this because I served in the former JNA, and I'm quite familiar with all of these weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, let's go to this photo. We had to start with a new one because once you save one of these other -- the one we did yesterday, it disappears into the record. So I don't think you need to draw the buses again, but can you tell us when the buses got there do you remember roughly what time of day it is at that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not fully certain, but it was in the afternoon, towards the evening maybe even. I'm not sure. The sun was still up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when -- what happened after you got there? What did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They brought us there in buses and we stopped in front of the warehouse. The first bus was parked close to the first entrance, the one right here. I was on the first bus. The second bus parked behind the first bus. We were given orders to run out of the bus as quickly as possible and enter the warehouse through the first entrance. I can point out if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Why don't you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was on the left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If you could take that marker again and just point with an -- or just draw in an arrow where you went into the warehouse as you recall. And you will get some help with that marker.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you put a little arrow on -- on that -- a little point on the arrow so we see which direction you're going in for sure?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. By your arrow, it looks like you're going into the entrance and turning towards the left; is that right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And as you went into the -- as you got off the bus and went into the warehouse, did you notice anything or do you remember noticing anything at that other side of the warehouse, towards where the buses were facing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were just Serb soldiers there, ordering us to leave buses as quickly as possible and enter the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And when you went into the warehouse where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can draw where I was, where I was in the warehouse. Do you want me to?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why don't you just put an X on the roof. We know you weren't on the roof, but that will give us an idea roughly where you were in the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And do you remember what was -- what was in there when you -- when you went in there, what you noticed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the very entrance, in the middle, there was a car turned upside down and set on fire, and there was a container, a large container next to the wall. And then in front of us at the very entrance there was some kind of a fence, a wire, all broken down. So there was a large opening and the wire was all demolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This fence, was that inside the warehouse, this wire fence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, inside the warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you draw a line as best you could the -- where that fence was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And you said -- you described a car and just to make it clear, was that car burning or -- it may have been the translation, or was it a burnt-out car?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't burning, it was burnt. There was nothing left of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you remember any -- any other -- anything inside the warehouse, any structures or things or items?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, I didn't notice anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Was there anything you later climbed up on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as I have said, there was that container close to the wall, and this is how I jumped through the window because I first climbed on the container.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Yeah, we'll get to that. Okay. So when you go in, where did the other people on your bus go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They also went into the same portion, same section of the warehouse where I was. The same applies to the people from the second bus. I was among the first ones to enter, and then after me a lot of other people came in, or rather, came in running, so that the section where I was was completely full.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, did -- do you know if people besides those two bus loads came into your side of the warehouse?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, later on. But I naturally didn't know where they had come from, from which direction, because I was already inside. Yes, a lot of people came in running until it was completely full of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How long did this process of new -- of new people -- I guess Muslim men, I take it, how long did this process of new Muslims coming into the warehouse last, if you can give us a rough estimate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, roughly -- I don't know exactly, but in my view, perhaps, hour and a half to two hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And how full did this area get between this -- this fence and the -- and the walls of the warehouse where you were?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was full of people. Tightly packed. We were ordered to sit down. We had to sit down. People were tightly packed; they were literally sitting shoulder to shoulder, and it was so full that we were almost suffocating. Everything was full. All the way up to the entrance, to this entrance here, this first entrance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Have -- can you give us a -- your rough estimate of how many Muslim men were packed into the warehouse when it was full? Your part of the warehouse, that is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about two and a half thousand to 3.000, roughly. I don't know the exact number. That was my estimate at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. How about guards? Could you make out any guards, any Serb guards from where you were packed in there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally there were a number of them. Occasionally they would come in, go out. They were moving around. First a civilian came in who threw Marlboro cigarettes to us. He took a carton of cigarettes and then threw cigarettes to people and whoever managed to grab a cigarette was allowed to light it up. After that the order came for the people who had money, jewelry, valuables on them to come out. They confiscated that from us; they took it from me as well. I had some gold on me. Even though some had already been taken away from me back at the meadow in Sandici, gold also. So the last gold bits that I had I surrendered to this man here. A lot of other people came out surrendering money, gold, watches. And they noted it down, they recorded it, saying allegedly that they would eventually return it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Aside from this civilian guy that gave you cigarettes, were there military-type people or people in uniform around as well doing this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally, yes, there were. They could occasionally come in, walk in front of us. They took out whoever they wanted to take out. They took out two men. They ordered them to stand against the wall. This wall here where I entered, on the left side. This wall here. This is the wall that they stood against.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why don't you -- sorry. Since you have pointed, why don't you just put W against the wall that you saw them being put against.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then what happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They questioned them about some villages, about some Serb soldiers who were killed. I didn't hear what they asked them. I know that it had to do with some villages and some Serb soldiers who were killed. And then again -- or rather, they interrogated them for a brief period of time, they yelled at them, but they didn't touch them. Then they ordered them to sit down again in their group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What sorts of clothes were the -- these -- the Serbs wearing, besides this civilian guy that you already talked about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of them had camouflage, multi-coloured uniforms. That is to say they were well-dressed. New uniforms. One among them had a UN helmet, the blue one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, the camouflage, what colour camouflage, roughly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Green.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, after that period where valuables were taken and these two men were interrogated, what's the next thing you remember happening while you were in there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After that, after the gold was confiscated, they would bring some water to us in a white bucket, and people were pushing everybody to get to the water. I maybe managed to get a sip of water twice because people were so tired and exhausted that there was almost a fight that broke out because of the water. Then everything calmed down and after a certain period of time I saw that the Serb soldiers became agitated and angry. They would go in and go out and then I heard shooting outside. I don't know where the shooting came from, but it was outside, not inside. They were so angry that two of them came in wanting to shoot at us. The man in the blue UN helmet and the other one who had curly, shoulder-length hair and black glasses, they had automatic rifles on them, and they pointed their rifles towards us. Then another soldier came in, and didn't allow them to shoot at us. He said, "These people are not to blame for anything." And then they went out. That is to say they listened to him, they obeyed him. Then they went out --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me stop you there a bit. You said that before you heard this shooting that the -- the Serb guards became agitated. Can you describe what you mean by "agitated"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: My opinion was that they were going to kill all of us, that they would start shooting at us and kill all of us. They didn't do it at that moment, and then there was this shooting outside and I heard screams and moans. I don't know where it was taking place. It was outside. The shooting was so intense we could hear shells landing all around. Here, where the asphalt is, from this direction I saw that the anti-aircraft gun fired towards the forest. I heard the firing of the tank and Praga. I'm quite familiar with these sounds. There was also fire from anti-aircraft machine-gun. And then it calmed down somewhat. They came inside and they said to us, "See what your people are doing. We created a corridor for them so that they could pass through it and look what they're doing at us. Look what they're doing to us." To this day I don't know who initiated that shooting and what was going on. After all of that calmed down, they ordered two Muslims from the warehouse to go out to bring in their wounded soldier. They went out, they didn't stay out long, perhaps a couple of minutes, and then they came back. And I didn't hear anybody asking them anything, whether they had brought in anybody or anything. They just came in calmly and they sat, but not near me. They were to my left. So I couldn't hear whether they said anything about what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I want to go back, just a couple of clarifying questions. Again, when you -- you've said before the shooting started that the guards were agitated. Can you describe what you mean by agitated? How do you know they were agitated? What were they doing, what were they saying, if anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were shouting at us. They were saying, "Look, we allowed your people, Muslims, to pass peacefully through," as they had opened a corridor to Tuzla, but they didn't respect that and the Muslims attacked the warehouse, something like that. And that the Muslims were firing and that naturally they were defending themselves, and that's why there was this shooting. I don't know what happened; it was never clear to me. Even now it's not clear to me. It's just that at one point I noticed that they were angry. These two first soldiers who came in, they wanted to shoot at us, but then this other soldier prevented it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. What I want to try to clear up is, did the soldiers get agitated before this shooting started, or was it after the shooting started that -- that you are talking about? Did the soldiers get upset or agitated before this shooting started that you heard outside?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the shooting, of course. They were angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how do you know they were angry?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could see them entering angrily with their teeth clenched, nodding their heads, shouting at us. I could see that they pointed their rifles at the group that I was in, and I thought that they were going to fire. But then this other soldier came in who prevented this. He stopped them from shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Had -- at this point when they had become angry and were shouting at you, had this been a change of the environment since the time that they were giving you water? Had there been some sort of change or was it pretty consistent the whole time, the way they were treating you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were pretty consistent. They were kind to us in the beginning; they gave us cigarettes, they brought water. Then after a certain amount of time, I don't know how long, they just changed their behaviour. Suddenly they became angry. I thought that something was going to change, but I didn't know what was going to happen. What their opinion was, I don't know. At one point though just they became angry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And after they had become angry for some reason, is that when the shooting started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shooting began after they became angry, and the shooting went on for about half an hour, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you describe the calibre of weapons you heard being fired, what kind of weapons you heard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Automatic weapons, an 84. I could see which soldiers had the 84s in their hands, automatic rifles, machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How were you able to see anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the shooting I saw that. They were going in and out, and they were all armed. So I saw them with the 84s in their hands, the automatic rifles, the machine-guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is an 84 a hand-held machine-gun?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. It's heavier and bigger than an automatic rifle. It also fires bursts of fire and you can have the ammunition belt with it. It can fire for a long time. You can load up to 150 bullets on to that weapon. It has its own magazine with the ammunition belt, so when you start firing, the ammunition belt goes through and spends the ammunition. So it's much more powerful than an automatic rifle or just a regular machine-gun.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So when this shooting started, could you hear automatic rifle fire and this 84 rifle fire, or 84 machine-gun fire?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Automatic rifles too. Machine-gun and automatic rifle have the same sound almost. The 84 has a slightly different sound. I even heard a tank firing, an anti-aircraft, 23-millimetre weapon, a Praga, and you could hear loud detonations of grenades. The detonations were so powerful that I was able to hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you say this went on for about how long?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: About half an hour, approximately. I don't know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. McCloskey. For the record, accused Nikolic is present in the courtroom now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you had said one of your -- your guards had made a comment to you about, "Look what's happening," something to that effect. When in this time period did this guard make this comment to the group?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said it when they brought the wounded person. Those two men, Muslims, who were ordered to go out and bring in their wounded, that's what they told them. They didn't stay long; they returned inside. They started to shout at us, things quieted down a bit, but even though later there was also some more shooting from automatic weapons, they told them, "Well, look, we let you pass through peacefully. We opened a corridor for you, for you to go quietly and peacefully to Tuzla and you don't want to do that. They are attacking us. Look at what they're doing to us." That's all that I heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how soon after all this loud firing were these comments about a Muslim attack made?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It all happened when the firing would lull down a bit, when the wounded person was brought in. I could see them firing in front, here in front of this entrance. I could see that from inside, how they were firing from automatic rifles. They were firing in that direction there, to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you put an F where you saw a soldier firing or a person firing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you -- were you able to make out the direction he -- he was firing his weapon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw from the inside a soldier firing there, and he was turned -- can I draw an arrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, why don't you put an arrow in the direction.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was shooting in this direction. [Marks]. In this direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Put an arrowhead on that, will you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was firing somewhere in the woods. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you put an arrowhead again so we can see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we need to see Mr. McCloskey. We need to see the witness making or drawing the arrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we have the arrow there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said you think he was firing in the woods in that direction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was firing to the right side. I didn't see if he was firing into the air. There was a panic among the people. We were all in a panic. We were frightened. And I could see him firing over there from our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let me -- when this sudden firing occurred from these automatic weapons, do you recall what, if anything, the guys that were guarding you did, if you could see anyone at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I could see them, they were moving around in front. They were coming inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did they appear like they reacted to this firing in some way, in any sort of panic or in any other way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I noticed that they were also frightened, the soldiers. They were in a big panic as well. I noticed that they were so agitated you couldn't really tell who was going where. And all of this was going on in front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You told us they were agitated before the firing started. Was there a change in their behaviour and their agitation after this firing started?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When the firing was going on they all went outside. No one was inside, they were just out in front. Of course their behaviour changed, they were angry, mad.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So after this half an hour period of all this firing going on, what's the next thing that you remember happening?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After the shooting everything became quiet, we were quite afraid, we were in a panic, we didn't know what was going on outside. Then things quieted down. After some time they came inside and two of them, the one with the black glasses and long, shoulder-length, curly hair, black hair, and the other one who had a blue UN helmet, and he was also wearing a bullet-proof vest and a camouflage shirt. They were the first to open fire at us. Behind them more soldiers came in, five to 10 of them, but these two were in front, they were the first. I've already described them. And the two of them, the first two, opened fire at us. So I could see when the first one opened fire, the one in the black glasses. At the same time, the one in the blue helmet opened fire too. At that moment I immediately lay down on the ground. I saw that they would kill us all. And as I was lying down, I don't know what was happening, there was a lot of noise, smoke and shooting. I don't know anything. I could just hear the -- the hum. I don't know what was going on. And this happened intermittently. It was already dark. Night had already fallen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This person with the long hair that you recall shooting first, would you describe him as a soldier or civilian-looking guy?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a soldier. He was wearing a camouflage uniform, a flak jacket, black glasses, an automatic rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. When all this firing opened up at you guys in the warehouse, can you just as best you can describe what you can remember. I -- we don't want to spend a lot of time here, but just tell us as best you can recall how it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course I can. When they opened fire I was lying down. Immediately I fell down on my stomach on the ground, and I don't know how long the shooting went on for. I continued to lie down. After some time there was a break, a pause; it was quiet. There was no more shooting. Then all I could hear were moans and shouts and people calling out the names of their parents, their close relatives, people who were still not dead. They had survived, they were alive, but they were heavily wounded, perhaps. And then during the night there were several such breaks. I continued to lie down. They would make a break, rest, then come in again and shoot. However they -- however long they wanted to. Then when they stopped they would just then throw in a series of hand-grenades inside through the windows, one of these bombs fell three or four metres close to me and it injured me. There was a small piece of shrapnel that scraped my -- or grazed my back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So during these -- these pauses and then they would come back in and shoot and throw hand-grenades. How long did this go on that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It went on all night, this firing. But I wasn't inside the whole night. During the night I jumped out. They made breaks a couple of times. After a lull -- I have to say before that, and I didn't point that out. Before they opened fire at us, there was a man who was a bit disturbed and he was very frightened and he ran outside and they killed him right there in front of the entrance, and they said if anyone else tries to escape, he will be shot just like this man. Now I want to go back to what happened inside. During the lull, the break that they made or during one of those breaks, I managed to reach the container, going over the dead bodies on the other side of the wall. So I would reach that container two or three times, then I would go back and lie down where I lay down before. I was completely soaked in blood. I was completely covered in blood. I could sense that it was very warm. I was lying on my stomach and I felt as if I had some burning embers underneath my stomach. It was so warm, hot, from that blood. Again, I reached that container and I climbed on to the container and I saw that I could reach the window. Then I stepped from the container to the window, the window was very narrow, but I squeezed through and then I jumped on to the ground. When I jumped out and hit the ground, I heard from the cornfields, from this lower side, and I think you could see the corn here --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Why don't you put a C in the rough area where you jumped out.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You said the letter C?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah. That's English for "corn."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's sign off on this one. Let's put your number again, PW-111, and the date is now the 7th of February.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Above here there should be a C, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You've got a C. I see where you put the C. We'll go to another photo. If you could just put your code-name, PW-111 in the bottom right where you did it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Put a little W by that P, if you could.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then the date again, 2/7/07.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think that we can -- that's a wrap, that photo. And if we could go to the next one, which is 65 ter 1571.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know obviously what your next question is going to be, but it is my impression that when you ask him to put a C in the rough area where he had just jumped out, he was interrupted -- he was interrupted. According to what we have in the transcript here, he says, "When I jumped out and hit the ground, I heard from the cornfields, from this lower side, and I think we see the corn here." I take it he was going to tell us something -- what he heard from the cornfield or what he saw. Perhaps he can finish that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. And if we could get that next shot up, that will give us a little perspective of...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: While I was reading this, Judge Kwon has found that the -- what we see on -- on e-court at the moment is the same photo with some markings. All right. So you saved it with all -- all right. Okay. No, because we see -- all right. Okay. Thank you. That's not a problem then. Sorry for interrupting you, Mr. McCloskey, but perhaps let's take the matter that I mentioned up, and let him finish his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As the President pointed out, I had interrupted you. Can you finish what you were telling us when you were coming out that window? You heard something, and -- and let -- just tell us the story first and then we'll get into what this photo means.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course, I can. I heard from the cornfields, when I dropped on the ground, I heard a voice saying, "There is another one jumping out." I didn't know that there were guards around the building. Had I known that there were guards, I wouldn't have dared to jump for sure. I thought that there was no one around, that -- and that I would manage to pull out or to get out of the warehouse. I didn't move, I lay immediately on my stomach and waited for them to kill me. I saw that I wouldn't manage to escape, to get out, because I heard the voice from the corn saying, "There is another one," and I knew that was the end of me, but I was reconciled with that. I knew I couldn't go further. So I remained lying between these two windows. I don't know exactly which ones, these two, three windows here. I was lying down on my stomach, turned with my head towards the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. You pointed out -- you said you weren't quite sure which of the two or three windows it was. Could you just draw us a big oval in the area, roughly, where you think you were below the windows, one of those windows?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can, of course. [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So you have drawn a big oval around three windows. Do you remember which one of those windows you came out of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I really couldn't say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then just -- you were lying underneath one of those three windows, as you've described. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you describe the -- how the cornfield was back in July of 1995? I mean, we see a scruffy old winter cornfield here, but just ignoring that, what was the cornfield like, you know, how high was it, how thick was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Corn was quite high. It was taller than me, about two metres. Maybe even more. Definitely taller than me. And in some places lower than me. It couldn't grow that high. The corn was still green, wasn't mature yet. The leaves were still green. And then underneath there were pumpkins. I could feel that as I was crawling through the cornfield.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's just leave that -- that photo alone. I think we've got the picture of where you came out. Can you just tell us -- and again I don't -- I know you spent some time in that cornfield, but can you give us the outline of what happened that night as you're in the cornfield, what you do? But just briefly.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was lying and when I heard the voice that I described a bit earlier, a soldier started walking through the cornfield. I could hear him walking. He came close to where I was. He pointed a torch light at me and fired a bullet at a distance of some two to three metres from me, hitting me in my right shoulder. He wounded me. I remained there, lying quietly, pretending to be dead. He asked me, "Do you want another one?" I just kept quiet, pretending to be dead. Most likely he concluded that I was dead and didn't fire at me again. A clip fell, his clip. He couldn't find it, so he called another soldier to help him look for it. They found the clip and then they went out of the cornfield. I remained there lying in the cornfield until the morning. In the morning, when it dawned, I didn't move so I was all stiff. The sun came out and it was a bit colder in the morning. I only had a T-shirt on me. Again I heard somebody approaching me through the cornfield, and I was overcome by tremendous fear. I continued to lie there. There were hundreds of flies on me. I was attacked by flies like I was a real corpse. I had a terrible odour from blood. Somebody approached me. I didn't see who it was; most likely he was a soldier. He came to about one metre from me. I slowed down my breathing so that he wouldn't realise that I was still breathing, otherwise he would shoot at me. He didn't see that I was breathing. He stayed there for perhaps a minute. He tore a leaf from a corn, and I could see him sniffling as though he had a cold. And then he went back into the cornfield. Then in the warehouse I heard somebody shouting. It was a man ordering for the wounded to be helped, if there were any wounded there. Allegedly the Red Cross had arrived and the wounded were supposed to be transported to the hospital to be treated there. Those who were wounded came out. Then I heard --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: How do you know they came out?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard them singing outside. They came out and they were singing together, because they were ordered. The soldier who ordered them to do that would start the song and then they would follow. It was a song about Draza Mihajlovic, and similar-type songs which I can't remember now, but all of them were about Draza Mihajlovic. And if they did not sing out together, he would stop them and start the song again, and they had to follow like a chorus. They kept singing for about half an hour, and then all of a sudden I heard bursts of fire. They killed them all. I didn't hear any songs after that. Then I saw them starting up excavators to load or to gather the corpses. I continued lying under the window.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The transcript said you saw excavators. Did you see anything as you were lying underneath that window?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the loader or the excavator, I heard it. I was unable to see because I was lying there next to the wall and I was unable to see it. I could only hear it when they started it. And I could hear the bucket scrape on the ground. I could hear the noise it produced. Then one of the soldiers said, "This one seems to be still alive. He needs to be shot." And then I would hear individual shots if they saw that somebody was still alive they would fire individual bullets if -- if one of the Muslims were still alive. After that I heard somebody shout that there were dead bodies around the building, and that they needed to be collected and then the other person said, "No, let's leave those alone for the time being and focus on those inside." And I started feeling this panic, that they would come to collect the bodies that were around the building. I started stretching, still in the lying position. I started stretching and moving about. I could see that I could move my arms and my legs. I turned my head slowly towards this building. There is another building, it said "pharmacy" on it. It was in red letters. And I saw two men go inside. I don't know whether they were soldiers or civilians, I couldn't tell. I didn't have time to observe that. Then after a short period of time, I crawled into the cornfield some two metres deep and then I continued crawling through the cornfield until the very end of the building. I went through a row of corn. There I saw two men who had most likely jumped out before me. They were dead, and they were lying below these windows on the left. Then I approached a river, I could hear the river streaming and I came close. The soil was a clay-type soil, and the corn didn't grow well there; it wasn't tall. I saw another two men shot in the head. They were dead. I crawled over them, I got into the river. I cooled down there a bit, had some water to drink. I crossed the river and then went into the cornfield on the other bank of the river and then I went into the forest, or rather, in the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you tell us what kinds of wounds, again, just tell us -- I know you've already described a bit of that, but what kind of wounds you actually suffered at the time -- the time at the warehouse that got eventually treated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I forgot to mention that while I was in the warehouse I was shot in my right leg, near my knee. And then when I jumped out, when I was on the ground lying on it, the soldier shot me, wounding me in my right shoulder, as I have told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think a long time ago you gave us your -- some medical reports of the treatment you eventually received for those wounds?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you always tell the -- exactly what happened to you, to the doctors and the people that asked you about how you were injured?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you always tell them the -- the absolute truth, that it was part of an execution?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told them the absolute truth. Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, let's -- I want to skip ahead a bit. Is it fair to say -- oh, well let's finish the -- if you could just initial this -- this photo as well and date it, and we'll send it off.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And we can close that one down. Thank you, Madam Usher. Do you remember telling an investigator at some point that you didn't always tell the -- the doctors about the execution because you -- you weren't sure you would get a full pension if you were part of an execution, something like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't quite remember it. It's not like I told every single doctor whom I saw the whole story. I just told them in brief terms. I didn't have the time to repeat the story to every doctor I saw. There was no need for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The question is rather more specific. In regard to any of these doctors that treated you, did you ever remember -- do you remember ever lying to anyone in particular about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go -- we'll accelerate a bit now, if we could. Is it fair to say that you were able to get back into the woods and meet up with some other people and work your way towards Zepa mostly at -- at night and arriving in the Zepa area roughly seven or eight days from that morning that you got -- crawled out of the cornfield?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I got out of the warehouse it was the 14th of July, 1995. I went into the woods. During that day I didn't have a watch on me, so I didn't know what time it was, but it could have been in the afternoon. I was alone in the woods. On that day I sat under a tree and it became cold, it started raining and hailing, but not for a long time. Then the weather calmed down, I continued my journey. I used the asphalt road to orient myself, and I went back to the same road on which the column had come, from Srebrenica, to the place where I saw people killed by shells, Muslims. I found some new clothes there, I changed, and I found some food. I found three men there, one of whom I knew. He was my neighbour in Srebrenica. He lived nearby. His name was Djeri; rather, that was his nickname. I didn't know the other two men. It was already getting dark. It was dusk. The three of them and I searched briefly through the back-packs. There were a lot of dead people, hundreds of dead people killed by shells, automatic weapons. We gathered some food. I found new clothes. I changed. The three of them helped me quite a bit. They bandaged my wounds. Then we moved away from there to spend the night somewhere. One of the three men had a brother there who was wounded. He was hit by shrapnel in his right leg. He couldn't walk and he remained there, lying among the dead bodies. We stayed there for two days. Occasionally, two to three times a day, we would go back to him, bring water and food to him, talk to him. We didn't dare stay long there, and then we would leave him again. On the third day we decided to leave him. We didn't dare tell him that. We left a pistol and a hand-grenade with him so that he could kill himself in case the Serb soldiers came across him, so that they wouldn't torture him and he could kill himself, and we left him. We didn't tell him where we were going. That was one of the hardest things for me. The fact that we had to leave this man alive, a man we couldn't help. We went towards Srebrenica, back to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I understand that has always been a difficult part of this -- this story. I didn't mean to skip it. But if we could try to go question and answer and if that would be okay, could we -- could we briefly describe -- I know this difficult trip and get to Zepa, Witness? Can you give us a brief account of how you made it through the -- well, tell us first of all why did you decide to go towards Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we were moving back to the Srebrenica area, during the day, as we were going back I came across a group of people, including my uncle. I met him on that road. They were also hiding there for a couple of days. They couldn't pass through because of the shells. I stayed for two days there with him because of the shells. The shelling was quite intense in the area that we were supposed to pass through. During a lull, when the shelling stopped, we managed to cross through that territory. We reached the Srebrenica area. We came to Jaglici again. I passed near an UNPROFOR check-point, or rather, there used to be an UNPROFOR check-point there. There was nobody there now. It was already dark.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Witness. I know this is not easy, but you've got to try to answer -- answer my questions. And as best you can, and we'll -- we want you to -- we want to hear the story, but you've got to try answer my questions. Where did you decide to go? Which direction did you decide to go in now?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the group that we came across there were maybe a dozen people there. We heard from them that Zepa had not yet fallen, that it was still under Muslim control, that area was still controlled by Muslims. So we decided to go to Zepa and we set out towards Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us about that, but if you -- I -- we've got a lot of material, and important material to go through, so if you could try to tell us as best you can about that journey, but we -- we can't get into all the details, I'm sorry. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. We passed through Muslim villages, Buce, Suceska. We passed through that area, Podravanje. We crossed Podravanje during the night. We crossed through Podravanje and we entered a large forest. Another group had gone through there before us and we found them sleeping in the forest near a canyon called Crni Potok, which is in the vicinity of Zepa. We met up with them. We stayed there a bit. They remained there sleeping, and we journeyed on. This was just before the dawn. We came to the Crni Potok canyon. We ate there. We descended down into the canyon and it took us some two hours to descend to the bottom of the canyon. We came to the river. We found a lot of people there, cooling themselves in the river, taking rest. We rested a bit, and then continued the journey towards Zepa. We came to Vukoljin Stan there were civilians awaiting us there, civilians and soldiers. We came to their kitchen in Vukoljin Stan. They gave us food there. We rested there. There were a lot of people there who had arrived before us. Also people from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What side were the soldiers that you came to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And do you -- can you give us a rough idea of how many days it took you to make your way across country to this place?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can give you a rough estimate. I set out on the 14th from Kravica, and somewhere around the 17th I arrived in Zepa. I'm not fully certain that the date is correct. This is just a rough estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And when you came to the soldiers and got some food, what -- what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was there the whole day, to the evening. The night -- the darkness fell, and another soldier who was there who had a car, a yellow Fica, Fiat, he was from Zepa. He was ordered to take me and another man who was wounded on his right arm to the hospital in Zepa that evening, and he did. We arrived during the night at the Zepa hospital. We stayed there for some time. There were a lot of wounded people in the hospital. Then the order came that we had to be evacuated from the hospital because, as they told us, they were worried that on the following morning the Serb soldiers would target the hospital, shell the hospital. So during the night they put us on a truck and then they took us to a village nearby and found accommodation for us in various houses. There were another two men with me, this friend of mine who was wounded in his arm, and then another man whose throat had been cut. We spent some time there, five to seven days approximately, in that house. They changed our bandages there, gave us shots, brought us food. They did this regularly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. It's break time, so it's a good time to stop, if I could interrupt you. We'll be back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, if this is break time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I know. I'm just making a -- recording this in my notes. So we will have a 25-minute break, starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We left off and you had told us you had been treated in a -- in some houses that were -- for about five to seven days that were nearby the hospital of Zepa. Can you tell us where the hospital of Zepa is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The hospital is in the centre of Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And after these five to seven days of being treated, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I decided with my colleague, who was with me in the room, I decided to go the mountain where the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina was. There were some civilians, women, young girls, men. We agreed that in the morning, at dawn -- we didn't want to leave during the night. Actually, we were afraid that there would be strong shelling in the morning, so that we wouldn't be able to get out. Before that, that day before we left for the mountain, my doctor, who was treating me, told us that the seriously wounded had to be evacuated to Tuzla. I was among the seriously wounded. My colleague also. But we didn't dare wait for dawn. We decided to go to the mountain, and we did go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So at dawn when you went to the mountain, what happened then?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were at the mountain for a while. Then we decided to go to Vukoljin Stan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what mountain, where was in relation to the centre of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's above Zepa. I don't know the name of the mountain. It's above Zepa. It took us a long time at night to get there, going uphill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then I interrupted you, and then you decided to go somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went from the mountain to Vukoljin Stan again, to the kitchen where we had come from Srebrenica, where they received us. That's where I found my uncle again, and many other people. I stayed there briefly with them. This colleague of mine had some cousin who was married in Krusev Dol, and he told me that we should go to visit her. And we went through some fields. We asked where this village was, and we were directed to the village. We found it. We sat there for a long time at his cousin's place. We had lunch. And we found out there that the first batch of the wounded had already been evacuated from Zepa in the morning. We decided as soon as possible to go back to Zepa, and we did go back. It took us a long time to get there. We came to Zepa --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So why was it that a day earlier you decided not to try to get evacuated with the wounded but a day later you decided to go -- try to get evacuated? Do you remember what changed your mind?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because I thought that it wasn't 100 per cent certain, and because of the shelling in the morning. Because they were attacking Zepa every day. Zepa was already falling. There were attacks all day long, and we were afraid to stay there in that house. We decided to go to the mountain before morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So then you heard about the evacuation, and where did you go?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We then went to the centre of Zepa, to the UNPROFOR compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What different forces or -- of soldiers did you see, if any, around the Zepa centre when you walked into it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: First the wounded left. We found that out when we came to Zepa, and of course we heard about it in Krusev Dol. That's why we went to Zepa quickly. Then we came first to the UNPROFOR compound, the UNPROFOR there were from Ukraine and they let us in. Then the French came, a doctor. They examined us, dressed our wounds. There was a Serb doctor amongst them, a soldier. He was wearing a camouflage uniform. He was also registering us, writing down the name of the wounded, and he was also examining, together with this other doctor, people, where they were wounded, how and so on. During the day we occasionally left the UNPROFOR compound. This was permitted. We went -- there was a water spring in Zepa in the centre of Zepa. So that's where we would go to drink some cold water. We would drink then we would go back to the UNPROFOR compound again. That day when we were examined by the doctors --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you again, but when you came in to Zepa that day to go to the compound, did you see any Serb soldiers?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course the Serb soldiers had entered Zepa. The evacuation was underway of women, children and the elderly. They were evacuating many, many people, and people from surrounding villages were still arriving. They were constantly arriving. Civilians were coming. And they were being evacuated to Kladanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you see the vehicles that people were being evacuated on?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did. Buses and trucks. There were many, many buses and trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When you walked to the centre of town to the Ukrainian base, did any Serb soldiers give you a bad time or stop you? Was there any check-point or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, none. We entered the UNPROFOR compound right away. They examined us there, and during the examination -- this went on for the whole day. It was very hot. My colleague and I boarded a bus with some other wounded civilians to go to Kladanj, to be evacuated. We entered the bus, sat down. Again this Serb soldier, doctor, came in who had examined us at the UNPROFOR compound. He let my colleague go, and he told me, "Take your jacket off." I took my jacket off. He could see that I was bandaged, and of course he saw that, he examined all my wounds in the UNPROFOR compound, together with the French doctor. He said, "You cannot go. Get out of the bus." And it was strange to me why I couldn't go. He told me, "You will be transferred by helicopter. Helicopters should come and you will be transferred safely." I was very sorry that my colleague could go and I stayed behind. I got out of the bus and went back to the UNPROFOR compound again. I was wearing a -- camouflage pants that I had found in the woods above Kravica when I came out of the warehouse. Most probably he turned me back because of those camouflage trousers. That's what I think. Had I had civilian trousers perhaps he wouldn't have. I don't know. Night came and again I went with some wounded civilians to the house where I was when I was at the hospital. And I spent the night there. I took those camouflage pants off, because I assumed that that's why I had been turned away. I found some track suit pants and I put them on and in the morning again I went back to the UNPROFOR compound. Again the French people were there. After that I saw Avdo Palo. He also came to the UNPROFOR compound that day. I happened to be near them, not in the UNPROFOR compound, but perhaps 100 to 200 metres away from the UNPROFOR compound, near the water, the fountain, as a green military jeep arrived. Tolimir came out; that's how he introduced himself. I don't know him before. With his escort of soldiers, they were armed to the teeth with automatic rifles, machine-guns. He negotiated with Avdo Palo. He asked Avdo Palo, Tolimir did, to order his soldiers to hand over their weapons, and that they would be transferred safely to Tuzla by helicopter. Helicopters were supposed to arrive. Avdo didn't agree to this. They were shouting at one another. I couldn't remember all that they were saying. And then after a while I walked off and they stayed there. I went back to the UNPROFOR compound again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you for a second. The person that you knew -- or that you are describing as Avdo Palo, what was his position at the time, as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was a commander of the army -- he was the commander of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And after that day that you saw him and Tolimir speaking to each other, did you ever get a chance to speak to -- to Avdo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did talk with him at the UNPROFOR compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was at the UNPROFOR compound.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: When was it in terms of was it before or after you saw him talking to Tolimir, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. The same day or another day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same day. The Red Cross came after that, to the UNPROFOR compound. All of us wounded were there. They started taking our names down, the Red Cross, and they were giving us some cards with our names on them, and they told us that we were prisoners of war. I objected to that. I said, "How can we be prisoners of war? Were we captured in any action? Can you see that we are wounded and we are in civilian clothing?" Had we been fit, we wouldn't have been there at all. We would be up on the mountain perhaps with the army. There were Serb soldiers there as well. They also mistreated us. They were telling us that we had once been Serbs. We originate from Serbs but we didn't pay attention to that. The UNPROFOR gave us water, they gave us packets of food. We ate. The French people were there too. The evacuation of civilians was in progress. Avdo Palo ordered us to rip up those cards that were given to us by the Red Cross. I didn't want to rip it up because I didn't -- I felt it was suspicious. Why would I want to rip it up? Some did rip them up, but I kept mine. I spent two more nights outside of the UNPROFOR compound in a small house. There were 12 of us who were wounded. The negotiations were still going on. Avdo Palo was negotiating with them, and he would inform us that we still couldn't be evacuated. I don't know why. I didn't ask him what he was negotiating about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you again. When you first had a chance, or you first spoke to Avdo Palo, as you know him, what did you tell him about your situation, if anything?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was sitting on a chair. I sat in front of him. I crossed my legs. We were talking. Normally, briefly, I told him where I had come from and what had happened there in Srebrenica with the people, how I managed to escape from Kravica from the execution, how a lot of people were killed in the woods or were captured. And he replied that he had already heard that from other people before. I sat with him. I saw him -- actually, the first time I saw him I didn't talk to him. The second time I sat down with him at the UNPROFOR compound. I think that if I remember correctly it was the last day. After that second day that I was there, I talked with him and I said, "Why is he there? Why doesn't he escape to the mountain, to the army?" I told him, "You will be arrested here by the Serb soldiers." He replied, "I don't want to leave until the last civilian and wounded person is evacuated from here. Let them arrest me. Let them kill me."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you said the last day. Can you tell us from the time that Serb doctor took you off the bus, how many days was it until you were actually evacuated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two more days, as far as I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And so the discussion you had with Avdo Palo occurred after you -- sometime after you saw that -- the doctor took you off the bus and sometime before the -- you were actually transported out of there. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He ordered us that day -- that was the first or the second day, I don't remember -- he ordered us, once the Red Cross distributed these little cards to us with our names, he ordered us to rip them up. He didn't believe in it. He said, "You are not prisoners. How can you be prisoners?" And he was shouting at them, "How can you treat them as prisoners? They were not arrested anywhere."

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Do you remember the date that you -- you signed up with the Red Cross?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do. It was the 26th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And you have provided a Red Cross document over to the -- to the authorities sometime after all this, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So can you tell us how it occurred that you -- you finally left this area?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The last day when I was sitting in front of Avdo, when I was talking to him, when I told him that he should flee to the mountain, that he would be arrested or killed, he told me, like I said before, that he is not going to do that until the last civilian and wounded person leaves Zepa, that he wouldn't leave. And that's how it was. The French managed to take away some of the more heavily wounded by putting them in those trucks and driving them off. I was asking one of those French people to put me into one of those personnel carriers that they were using and to get me out. He was speaking Yugoslavian and he told me that he didn't dare do that because they will come to a Serb soldier check-point and that the armoured vehicles would be inspected and that I would be taken off. And that's why he didn't dare to do that, and he was sorry. Again, I went back to the UNPROFOR, and I was waiting. I continued to wait. That last day there was a large crowd for evacuation of women, children, the elderly, and in the afternoon we left. I sat on the last bus from Zepa, and there were the 12 wounded and there were other people, elderly people, women, children. It was a full bus. In the neighbouring hills I could see lots of Serb soldiers. I saw many of them in the centre with us. They were speaking with us, but they didn't touch anyone, they didn't shout at anyone. They were just speaking with us in an ordinary way. They said, "We are not having a hard time with you wounded, but what are we going to do with those who are up on the mountain?" I told them, "Well, you go up there to them, up to the mountain to them." And they laughed. And then the time came and they ordered our wounded, us, the 12 of us, and we left the UNPROFOR compound. We boarded the bus. Avdo Palo stayed in the UNPROFOR compound after we left, and we were taken off in the direction of Kladanj. We were stopped again at Boksanica. That's not so far from Zepa, towards Rogatica. We were there for a long time. We got out of the buses. It was still day. An officer boarded my bus. I don't know who he was. He had an escort with him. And there was an escort who went with him. He wore a camouflage uniform and he stuck very close by him. He had a rifle called an Argentinian, I think it's of U.S. manufacture. He asked us who was from where and when it was my turn, I said immediately that I was from Srebrenica and he said, "How come you're here, all the way from Srebrenica?" I told him that I had come to Zepa to take food, to take food to Srebrenica so that I could feed the family. There was hunger there, and that's how I heard that the offensive on Srebrenica had begun and that I couldn't return to Srebrenica, and that's why I had to stay in Zepa. "All right," he said, and then he went on asking people, "Where are you from? Where are you from?" People responded. I heard him asking us all, "Do you know who I am?" Some knew him. I didn't. I said I didn't know. The people from Zepa naturally knew him. They knew that he was the commander of Rogatica. He asked us, "Do you know where Avdo Palo is?" We said, "We don't know." He said, "We arrested him at the UNPROFOR compound and we killed him." We just didn't say anything. We were silent. He left the bus and then he left. After being there for a while, it got dark. It was already night. I heard a helicopter land. I heard them saying that Ratko Mladic had arrived, but I didn't see him. I didn't see the helicopter either. It was far away from me. All I could hear was that it landed. After some time, it wasn't that long, the helicopter flew off again and left. And then after that, there was an order for the convoy to start moving, and the convoy started to move. They drove us towards Kladanj. We came and it was already the break of day. As we were driving it dawned, it got light. They stopped us at some place, it was a stop, and they let us get off the bus if we needed to go to the bathroom, and after some time, it wasn't that long, we went back to the bus again and the order was given for the convoy to start moving again and it did and we came to a place called Luke, close to Kladanj, and the convoy stopped there once again. The escort that was on my bus comprised of a Serb soldier from the military police. He was wearing a white belt. The French were also there from the UNPROFOR. Ukrainians, they were escorting the whole convoy. After some time we waited there for a bit longer, I didn't know what was going on. We were just waiting. Tolimir barged in. He just looked about the bus, he went outside, he was with his escort, a couple of soldiers. One of the soldiers barged into the bus. He had a paper in his hand and started to read. And all of the names of us wounded were there, and he read them out, all of our names. This and this person, this and this person, one after another we stood up and we got off the bus. Next to the bus there was another bus, and they ordered us to get into this bus, which had been waiting next to our bus, and it was turned in the opposite direction. And this was suspicious to me. We sat in this other bus and from my bus they were still choosing some elderly men who were fit. We all got into the bus, they drove us, and drove us. I didn't know where they were taking us. The people from Zepa knew the area. I wasn't familiar with the area, and we came to Rogatica. And I could hear those people saying, "Well, here we are, we've arrived in Rogatica." And in Rogatica we stopped at a warehouse.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... now, just to -- I appreciate your -- your account. I know you have testified before that -- and we want to try to go a little more question and answer. This -- the practice of this Court is a little different than the ones that you have done before. But let me just ask you a couple of questions about that. When you were a Luke, did everybody that got out there come to Rogatica or did some stay at Luke?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, naturally, there was a convoy of women and children. We got on to one bus and this bus took us to Rogatica, whereas the others remained back there waiting. Most likely they left, but I don't know what happened to them afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you taken to a prison in Rogatica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And were you there for about six months, abused, and finally released on 19 January 1996?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I know that that's a much shortened version of that experience, but that's not -- that is not the subject matter of this indictment, so I will stop my questions there, if I could. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Who is going first? Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honours. We have agreed I should go first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. You are free to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As my learned friend, Mr. Prosecutor, told you earlier, this system is a bit different from the one that you and I come from, it's based on question and answer system, unlike the other jurisdiction where you testified earlier. Let me ask you something else. Since you and I understand each other very well, in order not to overlap, for the sake of interpreters, let me ask you to make a brief pause before answering my questions. I would like to start the cross-examination by establishing some facts which first of all have to do with a number of statements that you have given so far to the organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina and to the international Tribunal. Let me start chronologically with your statements, just to make sure that we have all of your statements that you gave so far. Based on the records we have here, your first statement was given on the 2nd of February, 1996. You gave that statement to the inspector of public security station in Lukavac and that was the first time you spoke to a state official, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't remember the dates. To tell you the truth, I don't know when I gave my statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. If this can be of any assistance to you, we have all of those statements, and if there is any need for a statement to be given to you, I can provide you with a copy and then you can verify that you gave it and signed it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Except for that first statement, or rather, in addition to that first statement, another one was given on the 16th of February, 1996, and that was the statement you gave to agency for investigation and documentation in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which date?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: It should be the 16th of February, 1996.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possible. I don't remember dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Then according to our records, sometime in October, November and December of 1998, you met with Mr. Jean-Rene Ruez, an investigator of the OTP. You talked to him at that time. That was between October and December of 1998, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I talked to him, but I don't remember the time period.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. I just needed your confirmation that you indeed met with Mr. Ruez and gave a statement to him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now, there is another matter that I would like to clarify with you concerning these statements. They have different dates, they're practically three statements here. One was made after three days' worth of conversation, and then there were some other statements. When talking to Mr. Ruez, you also gave a statement that remained unsigned. In relation to this statement, you said that one of your friends who was either an inspector or was about to become an inspector was taking the statement from you, that he was basically preparing you for giving the statement, explaining to you how you need to give the statement and that later on you gave a statement to Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that, but I do remember giving a statement to this friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. That's all I wanted to clarify, namely, that you did indeed give the statement. Because this statement was disclosed to us by the OTP, so you do not deny that there is this statement that you gave to your friend who was a crime inspector?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I have to mention that this was not a detailed statement. I didn't go into all of the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. But you know, I fully understand that what you told us during these three and a half hours cannot be made to fit on to a page and a half, but what you said to that inspector was true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was most likely true. I don't remember the dates and I could have been wrong about some figures, because I gave statements before that and after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we will get to that. Now, if we can go very briefly -- [In English] [Previous translation continues] ... one brief period?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Witness, I have already put a similar question to you, but to clarify it further, when giving all of your statements, you always told the full truth to all of the people that you talked to, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And another question: Nobody pressured you to give this version or that version or to change, amend anything in your statements or to deliberately omit something. There was nothing of that sort, correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to begin with a statement you gave to Mr. Ruez, the OTP investigator. The statement begins you with saying, "I already gave a statement to AID and now I'm giving you some additional details that I may have omitted in my previous statement." Do you remember saying this to Mr. Ruez and that this was basically a follow-up to your previous statement given to AID?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-111 [Resumed]
